title: Fidelity Insurance: Per-route Credit & Insurance PRD
author: Marcos Alvarez
content:
Summary

This document defines the Fidelity Insurance product: a configurable per-route insurance and crediting mechanism that customers can purchase to protect against short-term fidelity regressions and SLA degradations. It blends pricing, risk modeling, and operational controls so customers can opt into automated crediting versus manual reconciliation.

Why this exists
- Customers have varying tolerance for temporary fidelity degradations (model quality or reduced feature surface) and for latency/availability blips.
- Enterprise customers request clear, predictable economic remedies that do not require manual dispute resolution.
- Current fallback and credit mechanics are reactive and ad hoc; Fidelity Insurance provides a pre-bought, predictable pool and ruleset to simplify billing and incident response.

Primary goals
- Offer a purchasable insurance tier that converts observed fidelity or SLO failures into pre-funded credits according to transparent rules.
- Integrate with per-route fallback decisions so the insurance product can be applied automatically when configured.
- Provide customers and internal teams a clear simulation and forecasting view showing exposure, pricing, and historical payouts.

Out of scope
- This PRD does not change low-level model quality detection signals. Detection will rely on existing eval captures and telemetry signals produced by the runtime.

Product variants
- Basic Insurance: flat monthly premium, small credit pool, auto-apply only to availability breaches.
- Fidelity Insurance: higher premium, larger credit pool, covers fidelity tier reductions and quality-regression events flagged by eval capture.
- Enterprise Custom: negotiable premium and cap, manual reconciliation option, SLA amendments.

Eligibility and configuration
- Sellers: Available for routes on Hosted and Dedicated tiers. Private deployments require separate negotiation.
- Configuration fields (per route): insurance_plan_id, auto_apply true/false, daily_payout_cap_tokens, deductible_tokens, observation_window_minutes.

Key mechanics (overview)
1) Purchase: customer selects plan and pays premium. A ledger record is created with an insurance_pool_tokens balance.
2) Detection: runtime or eval pipeline emits an insurance_trigger signal when a configured condition occurs for a route. Triggers include: availability breach over configured window, fallback to lower fidelity variant, or model-quality alert.
3) Adjudication: the insurance adjudicator evaluates the trigger against deductible and per-day caps. If eligible, it computes a credit amount in tokens and debits the insurance_pool_tokens.
4) Payout: the credit is recorded as an insurance_payout event and reflected in billing as a credit against usage in the next invoice cycle, unless configured for immediate invoice adjustment for enterprise customers.

Adjudication rules (initial)
- Deductible: each payout is reduced by deductible_tokens. Deductible applies per event. Example: deductible 500 tokens, computed payout 1500 tokens -> net 1000 tokens from pool.
- Per-day cap: do not debit more than daily_payout_cap_tokens from pool for a single route.
- Observation window smoothing: triggers require at least three samples in the observation window to reduce noisy alerts.
- Priority: if route has both Fidelity Insurance and standard credit policy enabled, insurance payout consumes first; standard credit events still emit telemetry but do not result in double-payout.

Pricing model summary
- Pricing inputs: historical fallback rate, route throughput (requests/month), average token consumption per request, chosen deductible and cap.
- Basic formula for premium estimation: premium = risk_multiplier * expected_monthly_payout_tokens * token_to_usd_rate. Risk multiplier accounts for uncertainty and administrative fee.
- Example: route with expected 10k tokens monthly exposure, token_to_usd 0.0005, risk multiplier 1.25 -> premium = 10k * 0.0005 * 1.25 = 6.25 USD per month (rounded and tiered in UI).

API primitives and events (examples described in words)
- Route insurance attachment: an API to attach an insurance_plan_id to a route and toggle auto_apply.
- Insurance pool ledger: an auditable record with pool_id, owner_id, balance_tokens, premium_charged_date.
- Payout event: event includes route_id, trigger_type, computed_payout_tokens, deductible_tokens, net_debit_tokens, trace_id, reconciliation_id. It must be idempotent and reference the triggering telemetry ID.

Console UX requirements
- Purchase flow: pricing estimator UI that accepts a route selection and shows recommended plan, estimated premium, and expected monthly protection.
- Pool dashboard: shows current pool balance, recent payouts, projected exhaustion date given current exposure.
- Simulation mode: allow customers to apply hypothetical triggers and see expected payouts before committing.

Operational responsibilities
- Product: plan catalog, pricing guideline, customer-facing docs.
- Billing: collection of premium and sequencing of credits on invoices; reconciliation pipeline owner.
- Runtime/Evals: maintain reliable trigger signals; provide trace ids and samples for adjudication.
- SRE & Routing: implement auto_apply hook and ensure decision latency impact is negligible.

Security, compliance, and auditability
- All ledger entries and payout events must be exported to the audit log. Exports must be encrypted and retained per the data retention policy.
- Reconciliation ids must be globally unique and include shard id and timestamp for write-once semantics.

Risk and mitigations
- Risk: high payout volume causing pool exhaustion. Mitigation: conservative caps and UI warnings with projected exhaustion dates. Optionally pause auto_apply when balance low.
- Risk: noisy false-positive quality triggers. Mitigation: apply smoothing and require corroborating signals before automatic payout.
- Risk: customers disputing adjudication. Mitigation: provide trace-level evidence and manual dispute workflow for enterprise customers.

Launch plan (milestones)
- Week 0-4: Pricing model prototype and UI mockups. Implement ledger service skeleton.
- Week 5-8: Integrate trigger signals from evals pipeline; implement adjudicator in beta with internal customers.
- Week 9-12: Pilot with 3 external customers, iterate pricing and smoothing parameters.
- Week 13+: GA: open purchase in Console, billing integration, full documentation and support runbook.

Success metrics
- Adoption: percentage of eligible routes with Fidelity Insurance enabled after 6 months.
- Reliability: proportion of payouts that required manual adjudication below 5%.
- Economic: average monthly payout ratio (payouts / premiums) between 0.3 and 0.8 in steady state.

Open questions
- Should insurance pools be shared across multiple routes for the same customer, or strictly per-route? (Initial plan: per-route with optional shared pool in Enterprise Custom.)
- How to price for private deployments where telemetry signals may be delayed? (Require manual negotiation.)
